levelTitle: Level 9 — Heap / Priority Queue / Top K
topic: Heaps, Priority Queues, Top-K and Selection Algorithms

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
problems.statement:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k-th` largest element in the array.

Note that it is the `k-th` largest element in the sorted order, not the `k-th` distinct element.

Can you solve it without sorting in O(n) average time?

examples.explanation: Sorted order is [1,2,3,4,5,6], second largest is 5.
Sorted order is [1,2,2,3,3,4,5,5,6], 4th largest is 4.
Single element is the 1st largest.
The 5th largest element is 3.

commonMistakes: Finding the kth distinct element instead of kth element in duplicate-preserving sorted order
Converting to Set which deletes duplicates and corrupts the rank count
hints: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest elements. The root of the heap is the kth largest.
Alternatively, Quickselect partitions the array around a pivot in O(N) average time.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=500 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=500 for complexity verification

problems.title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
problems.statement:
Given an `n x n` `matrix` where each of the rows and columns is sorted in ascending order, return the `k-th` smallest element in the matrix.

Note that it is the `k-th` smallest element in the sorted order, not the `k-th` distinct element.

You must find a solution with a memory complexity better than O(n^2).
constraints: All rows and columns are sorted in ascending order.

examples.explanation: Elements in sorted order: [1, 5, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 13, 15]. 8th smallest is 13.
Single element matrix.
Sorted order: [1, 1, 2, 3]. 2nd smallest is 1.
Largest element in 2x2 matrix is 5.

commonMistakes: Flattening the matrix and sorting, violating the memory complexity requirement
Binary searching on index rather than on value range [matrix[0][0], matrix[n-1][n-1]]
hints: The minimum element is `matrix[0][0]` and maximum is `matrix[n-1][n-1]`.
Binary search for the answer in the range `[left, right]`.
For a candidate `mid`, count elements `<= mid` in O(N) by traversing from top-right to bottom-left.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification

problems.title: K Closest Points to Origin
problems.statement:
Given an array of `points` where `points[i] = [x_i, y_i]` represents a point on the X-Y plane and an integer `k`, return the `k` closest points to the origin `(0, 0)`.

The distance between two points on the X-Y plane is the Euclidean distance (`√(x1 - x2)^2 + (y1 - y2)^2`).

You may return the answer in any order. The answer is guaranteed to be unique (except for the order that it is in).

parameterDefinitions.name: k
parameterDefinitions.description: Number of closest points to return

examples.explanation: Distance (1,3) is sqrt(10). Distance (-2,2) is sqrt(8). Since sqrt(8) < sqrt(10), [-2,2] is closer.
Points [3,3] (dist 18) and [-2,4] (dist 20) are the 2 closest.
Both have distance 1.
Single point returned.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N log N) or O(N) with Quickselect
commonMistakes: Computing square root Math.sqrt which introduces floating point imprecision and performance overhead
Returning empty array when k equals points.length
hints: The Euclidean distance is `sqrt(x^2 + y^2)`. Since `sqrt` is monotonically increasing, comparing `x^2 + y^2` gives identical relative order.
Sort points by `x^2 + y^2` and take the first `k` elements.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification

problems.title: Find K Pairs with Smallest Sums
problems.statement:
You are given two integer arrays `nums1` and `nums2` sorted in ascending order and an integer `k`.

Define a pair `(u, v)` which consists of one element from `nums1` and one element from `nums2`.

Return the `k` pairs `(u_1, v_1), (u_2, v_2), ..., (u_k, v_k)` with the smallest sums.

parameterDefinitions.name: k
parameterDefinitions.description: Number of smallest pairs to return

constraints: nums1 and nums2 are sorted in ascending order

examples.explanation: The first 3 pairs are returned from the sequence of smallest sums: [1,2],[1,4],[1,6],[7,2],[7,4],[11,2],[7,6],[11,4],[11,6].
The first 2 pairs with smallest sums: [1,1],[1,1].
All possible pairs returned since k > total pairs.
Single pair.

commonMistakes: Generating all N * M pairs causing Out Of Memory when N, M = 10^5
Re-inserting already processed pairs into the priority queue
hints: Initialize the priority queue with pairs `(nums1[i], nums2[0])` for `0 <= i < min(nums1.length, k)`.
Pop the smallest pair `(nums1[i], nums2[j])`, and insert its successor `(nums1[i], nums2[j + 1])`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification

problems.title: Find Median from Data Stream
problems.statement:
The median is the middle value in an ordered integer list. If the size of the list is even, there is no middle value, and the median is the mean of the two middle values.

Implement the `MedianFinder` class:
- `MedianFinder()` initializes the `MedianFinder` object.
- `void addNum(int num)` adds the integer `num` from the data stream to the data structure.
- `double findMedian()` returns the median of all elements so far. Answers within `10^-5` of the actual answer will be accepted.
constraints: There will be at least one element in the data structure before calling findMedian.
At most 5 * 10^4 calls will be made to addNum and findMedian.

examples.explanation: Single number 5 has median 5.
Two elements [10, 20]: median is (10 + 20) / 2 = 15.
Sorted [2, 6, 6, 10]: median is (6 + 6) / 2 = 6.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(log N) search + O(N) insertion for addNum; O(1) for findMedian
commonMistakes: Sorting array on every findMedian call causing O(N log N) latency
Using integer division instead of floating point when calculating the average of two middle elements
hints: Two heaps: a max-heap for the lower half of numbers, and a min-heap for the upper half.
Balance the sizes so that max-heap size is either equal to min-heap size or exceeds it by 1.
If total count is odd, max-heap's root is the median. If even, average the roots.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=202 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=151 for complexity verification

problems.title: Last Stone Weight
problems.statement:
You are given an array of integers `stones` where `stones[i]` is the weight of the `i-th` stone.

We are playing a game with the stones. On each turn, we choose the heaviest two stones and smash them together. Suppose the heaviest two stones have weights `x` and `y` with `x <= y`:
- If `x == y`, both stones are destroyed.
- If `x != y`, the stone of weight `x` is destroyed, and the stone of weight `y` has new weight `y - x`.

At the end of the game, there is at most one stone left. Return the weight of the last remaining stone. If there are no stones left, return `0`.

examples.explanation: Smash 7 and 8 -> 1. Stones: [2,4,1,1,1]. Smash 2 and 4 -> 2. Stones: [2,1,1,1]. Smash 2 and 1 -> 1. Stones: [1,1,1]. Smash 1 and 1 -> 0. Stones: [1]. Return 1.
Single stone remains.
Equal stones both destroy each other.
7 and 3 smash to 4; 4 and 2 smash to 2.

commonMistakes: Returning empty array or undefined when all stones annihilate instead of returning 0
Popping stones in wrong order assuming x >= y
hints: Use a max-heap to extract the two heaviest stones in O(log N) time.
If their difference is non-zero, push the difference back into the heap.
When the heap has fewer than 2 elements, return the remaining stone or 0.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Last Stone Weight II
problems.statement:
You are given an array of integers `stones` where `stones[i]` is the weight of the `i-th` stone.

We can combine any two stones of weights `x` and `y` with `x <= y`, yielding a new stone of weight `y - x`.

Return the smallest possible weight of the left stone. If there are no stones left, return `0`.

examples.explanation: Divide into two subsets [2, 7, 1, 1] (sum 11) and [4, 8] (sum 12). Difference is 12 - 11 = 1.
Partition into [26, 40, 21] (sum 87) and [31, 33] (sum 64) -> difference 5.
Single stone remains 1.

commonMistakes: Treating this as a greedy simulation like Last Stone Weight I (here we choose arbitrary pairs, so it's a subset sum partition problem)
Iterating forward in 1D DP causing items to be reused multiple times
hints: Any sequence of smashes corresponds to assigning each stone a `+` or `-` sign.
This reduces to partitioning stones into two subsets with minimum sum difference (0/1 Knapsack).
Find the maximum subset sum `<= total / 2`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Reorganize String
problems.statement:
Given a string `s`, rearrange the characters of `s` so that any two adjacent characters are not the same.

Return any possible rearrangement of `s` or return `""` if not possible.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.

examples.explanation: No two adjacent letters are equal.
Letter 'a' occurs 3 times in length 4, exceeding ceil(4/2) = 2. Impossible.
'v' is separated by other characters.
Single character is valid.

commonMistakes: Not returning empty string when the most frequent character exceeds (N + 1) / 2
Placing identical adjacent characters when placing the most frequent characters on odd indices first
hints: If any character count is strictly greater than `(n + 1) / 2`, it is impossible to separate them.
Sort characters by frequency.
Fill the even indices `0, 2, 4, ...` first with the most frequent characters, then fill odd indices `1, 3, 5, ...`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=390 for complexity verification

problems.title: Ugly Number II
problems.statement:
An ugly number is a positive integer whose prime factors are limited to `2`, `3`, and `5`.

Given an integer `n`, return the `n-th` ugly number.

examples.explanation: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12] is the sequence of the first 10 ugly numbers.
1 has no prime factors, therefore all of its prime factors are in the set [2, 3, 5].
The 11th ugly number is 15.
The 15th ugly number is 24.

commonMistakes: Checking every integer sequentially with prime factorization causing severe TLE
Advancing only one pointer when multiple candidates match (e.g. 2*3 == 3*2 == 6), generating duplicates
hints: Every ugly number must be generated by multiplying a smaller ugly number by 2, 3, or 5.
Maintain three pointers `i2, i3, i5` pointing to the indices of existing ugly numbers.
Next ugly number is `min(ugly[i2]*2, ugly[i3]*3, ugly[i5]*5)`. Advance all pointers whose product equals this minimum.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Top K Frequent Words
problems.statement:
Given an array of strings `words` and an integer `k`, return the `k` most frequent strings.

Return the answer sorted by the frequency from highest to lowest. Sort the words with the same frequency by their lexicographical order.

parameterDefinitions.name: k
parameterDefinitions.description: Number of top frequent words to return

constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
k is in the range [1, The number of unique words[i]]

examples.explanation: "i" and "love" are the two most frequent words. With the same frequency 2, "i" comes before "love" alphabetically.
"the", "is", "sunny" and "day" are the four most frequent words, with the number of occurrence being 4, 3, 2 and 1 respectively.
Only one word present.
All have frequency 1, sorted lexicographically.

problems.suboptimalTimeComplexity: O(U log U) where U = unique words
commonMistakes: Sorting lexicographically in reverse order when frequencies are equal
Using simple ASCII subtraction `b - a` on strings instead of `localeCompare`
hints: Count word frequencies with a hash map.
Sort the unique words: first descending by frequency, then ascending lexicographically.
Take the first `k` words.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=500 for complexity verification

problems.title: IPO
problems.statement:
Suppose LeetCode will start its IPO soon. In order to sell a good price of its shares to Venture Capital, LeetCode would like to work on some projects to increase its capital before the IPO. Since it has limited resources, it can only finish at most `k` distinct projects before the IPO. Help LeetCode design the best way to maximize its total capital after finishing at most `k` distinct projects.

You are given `n` projects where the `i-th` project has a pure profit `profits[i]` and a minimum capital of `capital[i]` is needed to start it.

Initially, you have `w` capital. When you finish a project, you will obtain its pure profit and the profit will be added to your total capital.

Pick a list of at most `k` distinct projects from given projects to maximize your final capital, and return the final maximized capital.

parameterDefinitions.name: profits
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of pure profit per project

parameterDefinitions.name: capital
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of capital required per project

examples.explanation: Since your initial capital is 0, you can only start project 0. After finishing it, capital becomes 0 + 1 = 1. With capital 1, start project 2 (cost 1, profit 3). Total capital = 1 + 3 = 4.
Take project 0 -> cap 1; take project 1 -> cap 3; take project 2 -> cap 6.
With capital 2, take project with max profit 3 -> 2 + 3 = 5.
Cannot afford any project with 0 capital.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N log N + K log N)
commonMistakes: Scanning all projects on every step O(K*N) leading to Time Limit Exceeded
Selecting projects based on ratio profit/capital instead of max pure profit available
hints: Sort all projects by capital requirement ascending.
Maintain a max-heap of profits for all projects that you can currently afford (`capital <= w`).
Greedily pick the maximum profit from the heap and add it to `w`. Repeat up to `k` times.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Maximum Performance of a Team
problems.statement:
You are given two integers `n` and `k` and two integer arrays `speed` and `efficiency` both of length `n`. There are `n` engineers numbered from `1` to `n`. `speed[i]` and `efficiency[i]` represent the speed and efficiency for the `i-th` engineer respectively.

Choose at most `k` different engineers out of the `n` engineers to form a team with the maximum performance.

The performance of a team is the sum of their engineers' speeds multiplied by the minimum efficiency among their engineers.

Return the maximum performance of this team. Since the answer can be a huge number, return it modulo `10^9 + 7`.

examples.explanation: Pick engineers 1 (speed 10, eff 4) and 4 (speed 5, eff 7). Performance = (10 + 5) * min(4, 7) = 15 * 4 = 60.
Pick engineers 1, 3, 4 with speed sum 17 and eff 4: 17 * 4 = 68.
Performance is 72.
Single engineer performance is 5 * 10 = 50.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N log N + N log K)
commonMistakes: Applying modulo before comparing maximums, causing incorrect optimal choice
Sorting by speed instead of efficiency: fixing the minimum efficiency first is required for greedy speed choice
hints: Sort engineers by efficiency in descending order. This guarantees the current engineer has the minimum efficiency in the team so far.
Maintain a min-heap of size at most `k` for engineer speeds to maximize the speed sum.
Calculate `speedSum * efficiency` at each step and track the global maximum using BigInt before modulo.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Smallest Range Covering Elements from K Lists
problems.statement:
You have `k` lists of sorted integers in non-decreasing order. Find the smallest range that includes at least one number from each of the `k` lists.

We define the range `[a, b]` is smaller than range `[c, d]` if `b - a < d - c`, or `a < c` if `b - a == d - c`.
constraints: nums[i] is sorted in non-decreasing order.

examples.explanation: List 1: 24 is in range [20,24]. List 2: 20 is in range. List 3: 22 is in range. Difference is 4.
All lists contain 1.
Must cover 1, 2, and 3.
Range [3,4] covers 5/1 via 5 or none? Wait, 2,4 covers 4, 3,6 covers 3, 1,5 covers ... wait, 3 is in [3,6], 4 in [2,4], but 1,5 has no number in [3,4] -> range [2,5] or [3,5].

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N log N) where N = total elements
commonMistakes: Stopping early before exhausting a list in priority queue approach
Not preserving tiebreak requirement: `a < c` when `b - a == d - c`
hints: Tag each number with its list index: `(val, listIndex)`.
Sort all tagged numbers.
Use sliding window to find the shortest subsegment that contains at least one number from every list `0..k-1`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Furthest Building You Can Reach
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `heights` representing the heights of buildings, some `bricks`, and some `ladders`.

You start your journey from building `0` and move to the next building by possibly using bricks or ladders.

While moving from building `i` to building `i+1` (0-indexed):
- If the current building's height is greater than or equal to the next building's height, you do not need a ladder or bricks.
- If the current building's height is less than the next building's height, you can either use one ladder or `(h[i+1] - h[i])` bricks.

Return the furthest building index (0-indexed) you can reach if you use the given ladders and bricks optimally.

examples.explanation: 0->1: free. 1->2: 5 bricks (0 bricks left). 2->3: free. 3->4: 1 ladder (0 ladders left). Cannot reach building 5.
Use ladders for jumps of 8 (4->12) and 15 (3->18). Bricks cover 5 (2->7) and 2 (18->20). Reaches building 7.
Use 16 bricks to jump 3->19, reaching last building 3.
No resources to jump.

commonMistakes: Using ladders greedily early on small jumps instead of saving ladders for the largest jumps
Forgetting that stepping down or equal height costs 0 resources
hints: Ladders should always be used for the largest height differences.
Use a min-heap to allocate ladders to the `ladders` largest jumps seen so far.
When the number of positive jumps exceeds `ladders`, extract the smallest jump from the heap and pay for it with bricks.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification

problems.title: Seat Reservation Manager
problems.statement:
Design a system that manages the reservation state of `n` seats that are numbered from `1` to `n`.

Implement the `SeatManager` class:
- `SeatManager(int n)` initializes a `SeatManager` object that will manage `n` seats numbered from `1` to `n`. All seats are initially available.
- `int reserve()` fetches the smallest-numbered unreserved seat, reserves it, and returns its number.
- `void unreserve(int seatNumber)` unreserves the seat with the given `seatNumber`.
constraints: For each call to reserve, it is guaranteed that there will be at least one unreserved seat.
For each call to unreserve, it is guaranteed that seatNumber will be reserved.
At most 10^5 calls in total will be made to reserve and unreserve.

examples.explanation:
SeatManager seatManager = new SeatManager(5);
seatManager.reserve();    // returns 1
seatManager.reserve();    // returns 2
seatManager.unreserve(2); // unreserves 2
seatManager.reserve();    // returns 2
seatManager.reserve();    // returns 3
seatManager.reserve();    // returns 4
seatManager.reserve();    // returns 5
seatManager.unreserve(5); // unreserves 5
Reserve seats 1 and 2 sequentially.
Seat 1 reserved, freed, then re-reserved.
Unreserving 1 makes 1 the smallest available seat for the next reservation.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(log K) reserve/unreserve with heap / binary search
commonMistakes: Pre-allocating a min-heap with 10^5 elements in constructor causing slow initialization
Scanning an array of booleans O(N) instead of using a priority queue for recycled seats
hints: Keep a counter `minUnreserved = 1` for the next virgin seat.
Maintain a min-heap only for seats that have been unreserved (recycled).
If recycled heap is non-empty, pop from it; otherwise take `minUnreserved++`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=301 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=201 for complexity verification

problems.title: Design Twitter
problems.statement:
Design a simplified version of Twitter where users can post tweets, follow/unfollow another user, and is able to see the `10` most recent tweets in the user's news feed.

Implement the `Twitter` class:
- `Twitter()` Initializes your twitter object.
- `void postTweet(int userId, int tweetId)` Composes a new tweet with ID `tweetId` by the user `userId`. Each call to this function will be made with a unique `tweetId`.
- `List<Integer> getNewsFeed(int userId)` Retrieves the `10` most recent tweet IDs in the user's news feed. Each item in the news feed must be posted by users who the user followed or by the user themself. Tweets must be ordered from most recent to least recent.
- `void follow(int followerId, int followeeId)` The user with ID `followerId` started following the user with ID `followeeId`.
- `void unfollow(int followerId, int followeeId)` The user with ID `followerId` started unfollowing the user with ID `followeeId`.
constraints: All the tweets have unique IDs.
At most 3 * 10^4 calls will be made to postTweet, getNewsFeed, follow, and unfollow.

examples.explanation:
Twitter twitter = new Twitter();
twitter.postTweet(1, 5); // User 1 posts tweet 5
twitter.getNewsFeed(1);  // User 1's news feed should return [5]
twitter.follow(1, 2);    // User 1 follows user 2
twitter.postTweet(2, 6); // User 2 posts tweet 6
twitter.getNewsFeed(1);  // User 1's news feed should return [6, 5]
twitter.unfollow(1, 2);  // User 1 unfollows user 2
twitter.getNewsFeed(1);  // User 1's news feed should return [5]
Single tweet feed.
Empty feed for new user.
Following oneself does not duplicate tweets in news feed.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(1) post/follow/unfollow, O(F log F) getNewsFeed where F is recent tweets of followees
commonMistakes: A user unfollowing themselves or losing their own tweets from their feed
Duplicate tweets appearing if a user follows themselves
hints: Always include the user themselves in the set of authors for `getNewsFeed`.
Store tweets with a global auto-incrementing timestamp.
Collect at most 10 recent tweets from each followed user and sort them (or merge k sorted lists).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=102 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=152 for complexity verification

problems.title: Find K-th Smallest Pair Distance
problems.statement:
The distance of a pair of integers `a` and `b` is defined as the absolute difference `|a - b|`.

Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the `k-th` smallest distance among all the pairs `nums[i]` and `nums[j]` where `0 <= i < j < nums.length`.

examples.explanation: Pairs are (1,3)->2, (1,1)->0, (3,1)->2. The 1st smallest distance is 0.
All pair distances are 0.
Distances: [0, 5, 5]. 3rd smallest distance is 5.
Single pair distance is |2 - 1| = 1.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N log N + N log(max - min))
commonMistakes: Generating all N*(N-1)/2 distances causing Memory Limit Exceeded
Binary search condition `< k` vs `<= k` off-by-one errors
hints: Sort the array `nums`.
Binary search for the distance `mid` between `0` and `max(nums) - min(nums)`.
For a fixed distance `mid`, count how many pairs have distance `<= mid` using a two-pointer sliding window in O(N).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=300 for complexity verification

problems.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
problems.statement:
Design a class to find the `k-th` largest element in a stream. Note that it is the `k-th` largest element in the sorted order, not the `k-th` distinct element.

Implement `KthLargest` class:
- `KthLargest(int k, int[] nums)` Initializes the object with the integer `k` and the stream of integers `nums`.
- `int add(int val)` Appends the integer `val` to the stream and returns the element representing the `k-th` largest element in the stream.
constraints: At most 10^4 calls will be made to add.
It is guaranteed that there will be at least k elements in the array when you search for the k-th element.

examples.explanation:
KthLargest kthLargest = new KthLargest(3, [4, 5, 8, 2]);
kthLargest.add(3);   // return 4
kthLargest.add(5);   // return 5
kthLargest.add(10);  // return 5
kthLargest.add(9);   // return 8
kthLargest.add(4);   // return 8
k = 1 tracks the running maximum element.
Sorted [-1, 0], 2nd largest is -1.
Duplicates preserved correctly.

commonMistakes: Re-sorting the entire accumulated array on every add invocation
Assuming initial nums has at least k elements (nums can have fewer than k initially)
hints: Maintain a min-heap containing only the `k` largest elements seen so far.
The root of the min-heap is always the `k-th` largest element.
When pushing a new element, if heap size exceeds `k`, pop the minimum.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=201 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=201 for complexity verification

problems.title: Take Gifts From the Richest Pile
problems.statement:
You are given an integer array `gifts` denoting the number of gifts in various piles. Every second, you do the following:
- Choose the pile with the maximum number of gifts.
- If there is more than one pile with the maximum number of gifts, choose any.
- Leave behind the floor of the square root of the number of gifts in the pile. Take the rest of the gifts.

Return the number of gifts remaining after `k` seconds.

parameterDefinitions.name: gifts
parameterDefinitions.description: Array of gift counts in piles

examples.explanation: In second 1, pick 100 -> leave sqrt(100) = 10. In second 2, pick 64 -> leave 8. In second 3, pick 25 -> leave 5. In second 4, pick 10 -> leave 3. Remaining sum: 5 + 8 + 9 + 4 + 3 = 29.
sqrt(1) = 1, so pile counts never change.
2 becomes 1, other pile remains 2. Total = 3.

commonMistakes: Re-sorting the entire array on every step instead of binary-inserting the modified pile
Overlooking integer overflow in sum when using 32-bit arithmetic
hints: A max-heap allows extracting the maximum gift pile and inserting `floor(sqrt(max))` in O(log N).
Repeat this operation `k` times, then sum all elements in the heap.

Stress test scale N=400 for complexity verification

problems.title: Total Cost to Hire K Workers
problems.statement:
You are given a 0-indexed integer array `costs` where `costs[i]` is the cost of hiring the `i-th` worker.

You're also given two integers `k` and `candidates`. We want to hire exactly `k` workers according to the following rules:
- You will run `k` sessions and hire exactly one worker in each session.
- In each hiring session, choose the worker with the lowest cost from either the first `candidates` workers or the last `candidates` workers. Break the tie by the smallest index.
- If there are fewer than `candidates` workers remaining, choose the worker with the lowest cost among them. Break the tie by the smallest index.
- A worker can only be chosen once.

Return the total cost to hire `k` workers.

parameterDefinitions.name: candidates
parameterDefinitions.description: Candidate window size from each end

examples.explanation: Candidates: first 4 [17,12,10,2], last 4 [2,11,20,8]. Pick 2 (tie broke by smaller index 3). Next pick 2 (from last 4). Next pick 7. Total: 2 + 2 + 7 = 11.
Fewer than 2*candidates distinct workers, so all workers are candidates. Lowest 3 are 1, 1, 2 = 4.
First 2: [5,4], last 2: [2,1]. Pick 1, then pick 2. Total = 3.
Single worker hired.

commonMistakes: Allowing head and tail candidate windows to overlap and double-counting workers
Tie-breaking: failing to prefer head candidate when costs are identical
hints: Use two min-heaps: one for the first `candidates` workers and one for the last `candidates` workers.
Compare the top of both heaps. If `headHeap.top() <= tailHeap.top()`, pick from headHeap and refill from `head++`.
Otherwise pick from tailHeap and refill from `tail--`.
